o: We must pick a common height H and build as many width-1 units as possible, where each unit is either one original plank of height H or a merged pair of two distinct originals whose heights sum to H. In Example 1, height 5 is achievable four ways (two singles, two pairs), so the answer is 4. In Example 2 no height can be formed twice, so the best is a single plank, giving 1. With n ≤ 1000 there are only O(n²) possible pair sums, so enumerating them all is cheap; heights can reach 2·10⁹, so use 64-bit sums.
k: The answer is max over heights H of (#single planks equal to H) + (#pairs summing to H).
Any pair sum and any single value are the only candidate heights worth checking.
n ≤ 1000 makes O(n²) pair enumeration trivially fast.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over Candidate Heights
a.i: For every candidate height H (each plank value and each pairwise sum), count how many fence units we can form: take all exact singles, then greedily match remaining planks into pairs summing to H using a frequency map or two pointers. This directly mirrors the problem statement.
s: Collect candidate heights: all planks[i] and all planks[i]+planks[j].
For each candidate H, count singles equal to H.
Count disjoint pairs among the rest summing to H with two pointers on a sorted copy.
Return the maximum unit count over all candidates.
a.t: O(n³ log n) — up to O(n²) candidates, each checked with a sort and two-pointer scan in O(n log n). Fine for n ≤ 1000.

a.n: Approach 2: Hash-Map Counting of Singles and Pair Sums (Optimal)
a.i: Since singles and pairs never conflict (a pair uses two distinct planks, a single uses one), the maximum count for height H is exactly single[H] + pair[H]. Precompute both maps once with hash maps and take the maximum — no re-scanning per candidate.
s: Build a counter of single plank heights.
Build a counter of all O(n²) pairwise sums (64-bit).
Answer = max(max single count, max over pair sums s of pair[s] + single[s]).
The answer is at least 1 since any single plank forms a valid fence.
a.t: O(n²) expected — one pass over all pairs with O(1) hash updates.
a.sp: O(n²) — the pair-sum map may hold up to n(n−1)/2 distinct keys.

w: Use Approach 2 in an interview; mention Approach 1 as the naive stepping stone. Pitfalls: forgetting the answer is at least 1 (Example 2), overflowing 32-bit sums in C++/Java (heights up to 10⁹), and assuming singles and pairs compete for planks — they never do since each plank is used at most once and the two categories are counted independently. Follow-ups: what if you could merge three planks (then a knapsack-style DP on counts is needed), or if n were 10⁵ (you would need FFT-style convolution of the value histogram to get pair-sum counts).
